Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege affecting many of the members of this honourable house. My question of privilege is based on a statement attributed to the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) which appears in the Globe and Mail of Friday, July 1, 1960:

On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of ihe Opposition):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Prime Minister whether he is now in a position to deal with the question which I asked him on Friday about negotiations with the United States regarding the use of nuclear weapons for Canadian forces, and which he said he would be in a position to answer today.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speechtext:
In reply to that question, Mr. Speaker, may I say this. I have reviewed the various answers given and statements made by myself since February 20, 1959. On February 20, 1959, as reported on page 1221 of Hansard, I set forth the views of the Canadian government with respect to this matter, and they remain unchanged. At that time I set forth, as I say, that the full potential of these defensive weapons is achieved
only when they are armed with nuclear warheads, and that of course was referring to Bomarc and other defensive weapons.
I followed that statement by a complete statement on January 18, 1960, in which I used these words, which are to be found on page 73 of Hansard:
In these circumstances negotiations are proceeding with the United States in order that the necessary weapons can he made available for Canadian defence units if and when they are required. I cannot comment in detail on these negotiations but I wish to state that arrangements for the safeguarding and security of all such weapons in Canada will be subject to Canadian approval and consent.
I want to make it abundantly clear that nuclear weapons will not be used by the Canadian forces except as the Canadian government decides and in the manner approved by the Canadian government. Canada retains its full freedom of choice and decision.
Since that time there have been continuing negotiations. By that I mean discussions between the representatives of the two countries. I am in no position to advise that there has been any determination made as a result of these discussions which would permit as yet of any negotiation taking place as between the Department of External Affairs and the department of state of the United States.

A supplementary question. I wonder if the Prime Minister could say whether the government has given consideration to abandoning these negotiations and adopting a policy of opposition to nuclear weapons on Canadian soil?

Mr. Speaker, in so far as general policy is concerned we are always in this position. On the one hand we are desirous of attaining disarmament; on the other hand we have to discharge our responsibility of ensuring to the maximum degree the security of the Canadian people. So far as that is concerned, discussions are taking place with respect to the Goose Bay and Harmon air bases, where an endeavour is being made to arrive at a formula which will ensure that Canadians in those bases shall exercise joint control. In other words, so far as these two United States leased bases are concerned, negotiations are continuing with respect thereto.
Beyond that I simply point out that as the hon. gentleman fully realizes, this is a subject which has exercised the minds of people

Inquiries of the Ministry everywhere in the world. Only the other day in the United Kingdom the leader of the Labour party, Right Hon. Hugh Gaitskell, if I might summarize what he stated, accepted the need of nuclear defence and also the fact that the onus for nuclear defence must rest upon the United States.

May I ask the Prime Minister a question based on his reply and based also on the statement made by the Minister of National Defence to the effect that at the present time negotiations are proceeding with the United States in connection with the storage by Canadian forces of atomic weapons in Canada for use either by United States or Canadian forces. My question is, in this connection is the Department of External Affairs participating in any way and, if not, what department is conducting these negotiations.

The use of the word "negotiations" is, of course, a material part of the question as framed by the hon. gentleman. What is taking place is that discussions are continuing between the Department of National Defence and the United States authorities in regard to this matter. When any basic agreement is arrived at in respect of these discussions then, of course, the Department of External Affairs will enter the picture and make the necessary negotiations to the end that notes may be exchanged.

In view of the statement by the Prime Minister that the Department of External Affairs is not actually a party to the negotiations in the sense that the right hon. gentleman has now paraphrased those arrangements, is it not a fact, however, that there is a representative of the Department of External Affairs who has taken part in some of the discussions between the two defence departments?
There will always be representatives of the various departments concerned, but the specific question asked was on the subject of negotiations.
I thank the Prime Minister for that answer. May I ask him which minister is in charge of these negotiations. Is it the Minister of National Defence or the Secretary of State for External Affairs?

In so far as the discussions are concerned the responsibility must necessarily be that of the Minister of National Defence, whose officers meet with their corresponding numbers in the United States and place before them the stand taken by the Canadian government, which is of the essence of any possible agreement in the future,


namely that if and when the Canadian government should decide to equip its forces with nuclear weapons, those weapons would be under Canadian control and would be used in Canada only as the result of a decision by the Canadian government.

Mr. Speaker, can the Secretary of State for External Affairs advise the house whether Canada has yet concluded the agreement with the United States with respect to the control and use of atomic weapons?

speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Secretary of Slale for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think that subject has already been fairly well dealt with this morning. The negotiations with the United States concerning the United States leased bases have not yet been completed.
Mr. Speaker, may I ask the Prime Minister whether the Minister of National Defence has reported to the cabinet in respect of these negotiations, and whether any decision has been taken?

Mr. Speaker, I have already made it perfectly clear that no decision has been arrived at. This is a subject that requires continuing consideration having regard to all the circumstances, on the one hand the need of assuring security and on the other the maintenance of that spirit toward disarmament which has characterized this government. When a decision is made, as I have said on more than one occasion, it will be brought to the attention of the house immediately.

speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REFERENCE TO REPORTED STATE- MENT BY U.N. SECRETARY GENERAL
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. member, as he so often does, has based his question on statements which he may think are facts but which in reality are far removed from the actual facts. In answering the question today I am not admitting that his premises are correct. The Canadian government has taken the stand throughout that the United Nations must be kept connected just as closely as possible with the disarmament negotiations. speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: REPORTED LOSS THROUGH OPERATIONS OF EXCHANGE STABILIZATION FUND
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Finance. Would the minister care to comment on an article in Saturday's Globe and Mail to the effect that Canada recently lost $101 million through the operations of the exchange stabilization fund, in keeping the Canadian dollar above par with the U.S. dollar?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: REPORTED LOSS THROUGH OPERATIONS OF EXCHANGE STABILIZATION FUND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I saw that article. It is an article that purports simply to be a paraphrase or to give the substance of an article appearing in a foreign periodical. Of the foreign periodical I have only this to say, and it applies to this article on their part as well as to others they have published. I do not know how a publication could go on publishing articles about Canada which are based on such total ignorance of Canada and Canada's policies. I would think it has got almost past the point now where that publication could offer ignorance as an excuse for writing the type of misleading propaganda of which they have been guilty.
As to this latest misleading statement on their part I have only this to say. The operations with respect to the foreign exchange control fund which have been carried on recently were completely in accord with the method of operation carried on by the Bank of Canada on behalf of the Minister of Finance ever since this government came into office, and prior to that time by the former government. There was no change in policy or in the basis of operation. These were simply normal operations carried out with a view to reducing the fluctuation in the exchange rate from day to day.
