maintopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS

speechtext: The house resumed, from Friday, July 1, consideration of the motion of Mr. Diefenbaker for second reading of Bill No. C-79, to provide for the recognition and protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the comparatively few minutes I had on Friday to deal with this very important matter I made clear, I hope, that we on this side approve the principle of this bill and will support its second reading so it can be sent to a committee, where we hope changes can be made in it which will make it a more adequate bill to accomplish the purposes that we all have in mind.
In that connection, Mr. Speaker, I have already made three suggestions concerning the improvement of this bill by amending the War Measures Act, which will give greater protection to Canadian citizens where perhaps they need more protection than in non-emergency circumstances.
We feel that the importance of this bill to accomplish the purposes we all have in mind, in its present form at least, has been very greatly exaggerated by the Prime Minister and that exaggeration of its significance can only mislead and raise perhaps unrealistic hopes, indeed leading to later disillusionment. The test of the government's objectivity in this matter, of its real appreciation of the importance and, indeed, of the complexity of the subject, will be in examining the procedure followed concerning' it and judging this against the procedures promised and the assurances given and the performance so far.
Let us look at the record in this regard, Mr. Speaker. The Prime Minister mentioned the desirability of a bill of rights and his decision to introduce such a bill into the House of Commons during the election campaigns of 1957 and 1958. In accordance with those election statements he did, indeed, introduce such a bill on September 5, 1958, some 19 or 20 months ago. This bill was limited in scope and, in its effect, declaratory only.
It should be made clear that that bill, and indeed the bill before the house today, bear no relationship whatever, notwithstanding what the Prime Minister now says, to the impressive and indeed eloquent proposals which he used to make and which he has brought to our attention already in the discussion of this bill, proposals which he used to make when he was in opposition about an

Human Rights
effective and comprehensive measure to protect our rights and freedoms. In those days he thought such a measure should be binding on all Canadian legislatures, thus protecting all Canadians against all acts of all governments which violated those rights. Indeed, in those days the Prime Minister used to get quite impatient with those who pointed out the constitutional difficulties in this field because of the division of authority and jurisdiction as between federal and provincial legislatures, each of which, of course, is sovereign in its own field.
I had something to say in the house on September 5, 1958 on the first reading of the other bill, and I ventured to quote some of the statements made by the Prime Minister in 1947 concerning what should be done in connection with the protection of rights and freedoms through parliamentary action. In those days, and subsequently, the Prime Minister proposed that representatives of the provinces should be called in so that the final result would be, he hoped, a joint federal-provincial bill of rights for Canada.
On May 16, 1947 in this house he said that human freedoms were not circumscribed by territorial considerations and he advocated, in addition to a comprehensive bill of rights, the repeal of the War Measures Act and a revision of the Official Secrets Act which presumes guilt unless an individual can prove innocence. He could not do those things earlier because, as he explained to the house on September 5, 1958 he was on the opposition side with a small membership. At this time, as he put it and it was certainly true, he said he was on the government side with no small membership. There is, therefore, no obstacle of that kind now in the way of a more comprehensive bill than the one we had before us, a more comprehensive approach to parliamentary protection in this field.
Furthermore, the Prime Minister once argued that if there were doubts about federal jurisdiction and what could be covered by a bill or an amendment to the constitution, if that procedure were to be followed, then let the supreme court give an opinion. On March 14, 1958, during the election campaign of that year, he was quoted as saying as follows, and I quote from the press report of his speech:
The Supreme Court of Canada would be asked to rule whether Ottawa has the power under the constitution to bring in such a measure. We want such a ruling so that we will encounter no constitutional obstacle when we bring such a bill before parliament.
Again on March 18, four days later, in Vancouver he was quoted as saying:
The Prime Minister explained that the bill of rights would be submitted first to the supreme court in the form of a reference.

We know that this was not done. Indeed, we have before us in this bill no proposal of any kind for a constitutional amendment even in respect of matters under federal jurisdiction alone. What we have is a normal piece of legislation to be passed in the ordinary way with ordinary effect and which, of course, could be abrogated or changed by any future parliament in the ordinary way. Without recourse to any of the procedures that were promised some time ago, this limited and purely declaratory bill was introduced. I am now talking about the first introduction in 1958. The Prime Minister asked for its careful examination by all who were interested, and indicated that suggestions would be welcomed. In his statement at that time in 1958, as reported at page 4644 of Hansard, the Prime Minister had this to say:
I can only hope that Canadians as a whole will give to parliament the benefit of their suggestions and ideas in the next few months so we shall be able to make such amendments in the bill to be presented to the next parliament-
That was the parliament of 1959.
-as will still the heart stirrings of those who fear for freedom in our country-[DOT]
Then he concluded his speech on this occasion by saying:
I hope we will be enabled next session-[DOT]
That is the session of 1959.
-to discuss this question again fully and completely, and that out of the counsel of parliament and the representations of our fellow Canadians, whatever changes should be made in this bill of rights can be made in the bill then to be presented,-
At that time, Mr. Speaker, when I ventured to speak-and by agreement there were only three speeches, one by the leader of each party-I had these suggestions to make. As reported at page 4652 of Hansard of 1958- and I mention this so that we can see whether any of these suggestions have been carried out-I said this:
... I have only three suggestions to make, one of which was put forward this morning by the Prime Minister on behalf of the government; first, that there should be the widest possible circulation of the bill to organizations which have shown an interest in this question and to individuals such as deans of law schools with requests for their views and comments-
I do not know whether that has been done, although I know that in the intervening period the government has received suggestions and comments. Then I continued:
-second, that there should be set up next session-
That is last session.
-to consider this bill a joint committee of both houses with broad powers, including the power to summon witnesses; third, and this is something even more important that might be done, that we should try to secure the support and co-operation of the provinces for any Canadian action in this field. Indeed, as a result of consultation with the

provinces it might be possible to widen the action so as to include both the federal government and provincial governments in a joint declaration on individual rights and freedoms. Then indeed we would have a powerful symbol.
We know now, Mr. Speaker, what has happened or rather what has not happened. The provinces have not been approached and were not consulted. Nothing was done in the last session of parliament. Then there was the Prime Minister's promise made to the annual meeting of the Canadian Bar Association in Vancouver last September. In a statement at page 94 in the printed record of that convention the Prime Minister said this, and I would point out that we are now into September of 1959:
From the chairman's agenda I note that one subject for discussion this morning is the bill of rights. It is my intention to have the measure to provide for a bill of rights introduced early in the next session of parliament-
That is the present session of parliament, nothing having been done in 1959. The Prime Minister continued:
[DOT]-and to have it submitted to a committee of both houses of parliament.
He also had this to say:
No one occupying the position that I do can overstate the benefits that come when the people of the nation give me and those associated with me, and through them to parliament, the benefit of their counsel and advice. Parliament will welcome any suggestions from the Canadian Bar Association in connection with the prospective legislation on the bill of rights. Indeed, the more attention given to an analysis of the bill of rights, the more beneficial will be the net result when the legislation is brought before parliament.
At this convention a resolution was passed on a report by the civil liberties section submitted to the bar convention. It indicated that in view of the assurance of the Prime Minister that this bill would be submitted to a joint committee, perhaps the kind of analysis which they were about to make might be superseded because of the possibility of their appearance before this joint committee. In the report to the conference-and I quote from page 192-the chairman of the civil liberties section, Mr. David W. Mundell, had this to say on behalf of his committee:
As explained to the attending members-
That is the members of the civil liberties section.
-at the beginning of the first session, Mr. Diefenbaker's bill is no longer a practical proposal since it will go before a joint committee of the house and Senate where it will obviously be changed from the ground up.
Therefore in the resolution of the civil liberties section, which was adopted, this committee came to this conclusion in that resolution:
Human Rights
Be it resolved, therefore, that this section on civil liberties recommends to the council and executive that appropriate steps be taken to ensure that the views of the association be presented to the joint committee as the opportunity may arise.
It would be interesting to find out whether any such opportunity is now about to arise in view of the fact that we have reached July and that it is not now possible, I understand-and the Prime Minister will correct me if I am wrong-to set up a joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons. Certainly no such joint committee as promised was set up previously in this session, although that procedure would have been possible. The Prime Minister decided not to follow that course but to postpone the introduction of this bill until July 1, 1960, Dominion day, when it could be brought in in the morning prior to the trooping of the colours in the afternoon.
As I have said, this bill has already been examined very carefully outside parliament during these intervening months. In that examination I think it is correct to say that the purposes of the bill have been universally applauded; but the reception given to the text of the bill which was introduced in September, and which is substantially the same as the bill we are considering today except for some changes, some of which are I think helpful and some perhaps can be considered retrogressive, was cool and in large part critical. Many suggestions have been made for improvement, particularly by the bar association, whose views were embodied in the March, 1959 edition of the Canadian Bar Review which devoted itself entirely to this bill, and which views certainly bear very careful examination by anyone who is interested in an objective analysis of the purposes and provisions of the bill.
In addition, a very impressive submission was made to the government on April 29, 1959 by 30 reputable and important Canadian associations, and that submission should be also carefully examined. Yet you will find very little of it in the amended bill. Indeed this is very surprising in view of what the Prime Minister said in his broadcast the other night, that this present bill contains some additions which have resulted from the views expressed in order to strengthen the guarantee of individual rights and freedom.
Anyone who studies the views expressed by the experts and the organizations will not be impressed by the changes made in this bill in order to meet those views. That is all the more surprising when we consider that such a measure as this needs the widest possible basis of public support in order that it might achieve its maximum usefulness and value. It is no great inducement for individuals and

Human Rights
organizations to come before a committee of this house, which presumably is about to be set up, and repeat their views when their suggestions have been so completely ignored by this government.
Then, Mr. Speaker, there is the question of consultation with the provinces. So far as we can ascertain, and we have tried to find out, there has been a complete failure to consult with the provinces and to explore the possibility of a jointly agreed declaration which might be inserted in the constitution. As I have just indicated, I urged the government in September of 1958 to conduct such consultations, and numerous groups and organizations and individuals have also urged that this course be followed. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that it cannot be denied that this would be the best course to follow.
The Prime Minister as recently as last Friday, repeating what he had said previously, threw up smokescreen of the impossibility of infringing upon provincial jurisdiction in this field. No one is suggesting that there should be any infringement upon provincial jurisdiction in any field. Such a binding and collective declaration would not involve any transfer of jurisdiction from one sphere of government to the other. It would mean that individual rights and freedoms would be as fully protected as they can be in this country by legislative action once the government has decided to proceed by way of such legislative action. Federal action alone will not cover the most important sector of human rights and fundamental freedoms under our constitution.
The Prime Minister also attempts to justify his failure-

maintopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman tell me what particular constitutional freedoms come under provincial jurisdiction? The hon. member made the statement that it would not cover that question.

maintopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext:
I made the statement that the whole field of rights and liberties falls under two jurisdictions, the provincial and the federal. Surely the Prime Minister, who is a lawyer-I am not-must know that the provinces are very jealous of the authority given to them by the constitution in this field; and if that is true, then federal action alone will not cover all the matters which come under human rights and fundamental freedoms. It does not cover legal rights or all the constitutional rights, and it certainly does not cover economic rights.
Surely, Mr. Speaker, it is a very unimpressive attempt to justify the failure to make any efforts of any kind to consult the provinces to say that such consultations would not be

successful, that the record of the past shows that, and that they would postpone indefinitely any action on this front. That is surely a poor excuse for not making at least an attempt.
Mr. Speaker, Saskatchewan, as we know, already has a bill of rights. The new Quebec premier, Mr. Lesage, had already stated more than once during the election campaign that he intended to present such legislation for the province of Quebec. No opposition has been expressed from any other province against such consultation and against at least the possibility of united action in this field. There is going to be a federal-provincial meeting at the end of this month in Ottawa; so why was it not possible, once it was decided to postpone this matter until July, to put this whole question on the agenda of that meeting for at least preliminary discussion? If no progress were made then it would be possible for the government to proceed with its own bill at the next session.
Well, Mr. Speaker, the government has ignored all these suggestions and has done nothing until July 1, 1960. The government even refuses to put in the constitution provisions-and they are in this bill-covering federal matters only, matters over which it is claiming full authority in this field. The excuse given by the Prime Minister, or the reason if you like, was that it would be no more difficult to change a constitutional provision of this kind than to change ordinary legislation.
That is true; technically it is correct. But what an argument to be used, Mr. Speaker, by one who admits that the main value of this bill is its moral and symbolic value; that its main importance is the deterrent and warning effect it would have on future parliaments which might be tempted to pass laws which would affect the rights mentioned in this bill. If that is its main value, surely that value would be greatly increased by putting these federal provisions in our constitution and giving them the prestige, the sanctity and the significance which would go with inclusion in the constitution. The government, however, will have none of this. The Prime Minister prefers to introduce an ordinary legislative measure-that is, ordinary in its procedural and constitutional significance-at the close, or what we still hope to be the close, of this session.
From this, Mr. Speaker, you can assess the purposes of those sponsoring this bill as a great national, non-partisan move in the field of human rights by the flat refusal of the government to adopt any other procedure; by the flat refusal of the government to adopt any other procedure even though that would have been better in every way, except perhaps

from the viewpoint of a government determined to push this measure through in the dying days of a long and exhausting session.
I ask, therefore, is this carrying out the assurance given in this parliament on September 5, 1958 which I have just read? Is this discharging the Prime Minister's commitment to the Canadian Bar Association to set up a joint committee of both houses, which I have also read?
Let us look for a moment at the bill itself and since this is second reading, the principles embodied in it. As I have said, there is no difference of opinion in the house about the importance of protecting and promoting human rights and fundamental freedoms. We all of us know that the price of freedom is eternal vigilance. We know also that it is the responsibility of freedom to provide among other things security for its citizens, including basic economic and social security, which cannot be said to exist in any country in which large numbers of its citizens cannot find work, as is the case in this country in July, 1960. Freedom from want and from the demoralization and deprivations of unemployment is an important part of the whole concept of freedom in our modern age, but there has been no mention of this by any spokesman for the government so far.
Furthermore, freedoms are not guaranteed by words, even words in a constitution, let alone by words in an ordinary, normal act of parliament. Earlier as well as contemporary history is littered with the wreckage of high-sounding declarations and bills of rights which were to guarantee so very much and last forever. But as Professor McWinney of the Toronto law faculty, writing in the Canadian Bar Review from which I have already read, reminded us, "Words alone are frail packages for human hopes".
Incorruptible and respected courts enforcing laws made by free men in parliament assembled and dealing with specific matters, with specific sanctions to enforce their observance; these are the best guarantee of our rights and liberties. This is the tried and tested British way, and this is a better course to follow than the mere pious affirmation of general principles, to which some political societies are addicted.

maintopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman permit a question? Does he regard the international declaration of human rights, which is in no way enforceable, as one of those wrecks?

maintopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext:
No, I do not. The international declaration on human rights adopted by the United Nations is a great landmark in international progress in this field, and
Human Rights
can be used as a means of advancement by those countries which do not yet possess human rights. But all those rights are, I think, already realized to as great an extent in this country as in any country in the world. What I refer to as the wreckage of high-sounding declarations are the declarations made by some countries in this world at the present time, and in the nineteenth century, about the inviolability of human rights and freedom, and then the refusal to implement any of those declarations by legislative or policy action.
Surely the Prime Minister, as a student of history, must know that there have been these wreckages throughout history. Indeed,
I have myself heard people talking about freedom and human rights in the United Nations and attacking a country such as France, which has been in the forefront of progress in this direction, because it has not gone as far as it should, according to those delegations; and those delegations came from countries at least one of which recognized legal slavery but which had subscribed formally to the international document on human rights. That is what I mean by the wreckage of high-sounding declarations.
Anyway, the problem is not whether we should protect our rights, but how to do it most effectively. This bill, it cannot be denied, cuts across our traditional practices. That does not necessarily make it wrong, because conditions change and circumstances alter; but it does underline the necessity of giving this measure the most careful scrutiny inasmuch as it is such a departure. We all recognize that the preservation of our rights and freedoms, as the very foundation of our culture and our civilization, depends primarily on our community itself, on its manners and morals, on its constant willingness to fight against prejudices and discrimination and arbitrary power. While this is true-and the experience of many other countries shows that a written law alone cannot adequately protect human rights-we agree that such protection may, in present circumstances, require from time to time new legislative and judicial safeguards.
There is, however, a wide range of opinion as to what those legislative safeguards should be. There are those who believe that existing provisions are adequate and that a bill of rights would not only be useless but might conceivably be dangerous. Professor Scott, who is an authority in this field, whether or not we agree with all his views-

maintopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext: A great authority.

maintopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext:
Yes, he has devoted many years of study to these questions-Professor Scott sums up that view, without agreeing

Human Rights
with it, when he says in his "Civil Liberties and Canadian Federalism", at page 13:
With Magna Carta in the background and Dicey's rule of law in the foreground, we have not seemed to need any further safeguard for civil liberties. And in truth, when we look at other constitutions with bills of rights in their written texts, not excepting the American constitution, and compare the rights of citizens under them with what has commonly prevailed in Canada, we have not felt that we were under any particular disadvantage.

maintopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext: Is that his view?

maintopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext:
I said that is one view, and it is a very good summary of the viewpoint of those people who accept it. Professor Scott has other views and he would go much further, as I shall point out later, than is gone in this bill. That is one extreme, the view of people who do not think we should proceed with this project at all but should stick to the tried and trusted procedures and not worry about bills of rights. At the other extreme are those people who are so anxious to have a bill of rights that they are ready to accept and support any bill on the ground that a bad bill is better than no bill; that a piece of bread is better than no loaf.
We on this side do not support either of these extreme positions. If we are to have a bill of rights not only to protect our own freedom but to serve as an inspiring symbol of the values we need to protect, it must be a good and effective bill for that purpose. We do not think that just any bill, irrespective of its limitations and inadequacy, will necessarily serve a useful purpose. The Prime Minister described his own bill in September, 1958 as a first step, and he confirmed that description on Friday, advancing the view that a first step, however small and timid, was better than nothing. Professor Scott, in the lectures from which I have already quoted, warned us against the danger of such a view when he said:
It seems to be assumed that a first step is always a good thing. Presumably a first step is a good thing if it is taking us closer to a desired goal and will be followed by a second step. But if the taking of the first step confuses the issue and discourages people from any further effort then it may not be a good thing. I am frankly afraid that this is the position we may be facing.
It will be our purpose on this side to support the motion to send this bill to a committee even at this late date, and do what we can in that committee to make this bill a more adequate and suitable one than it is now for the purposes for which it is intended. Certainly its present inadequacy has been exposed by many who have examined and commented upon it.
Perhaps particular attention-and I referred to this earlier-should be given to the criticisms contained in the special number of

the Canadian Bar Review of March, 1959, criticisms which apply to this present bill as much as to the earlier version. If you read the articles in this review and other articles written by men quite as sensitive as any hon. member of this house to the need to protect our rights and liberties, the Prime Minister's claims for this bill become extravagant and excessive.
Let us look at what some of these objective, non-partisan commentators have to say about some of the principles and provisions of the bill. Let us take only one paragraph from the article in this review by Professor Bora Laskin, of the University of Toronto, an authority in this field. I am sure it will not be suggested that Professor Laskin has any political axe to grind in making this comment:
Committed though I am to the thesis which is implicit in Bill No. C-60, the document is disappointing in its approach, unnecessarily limited in its application and ineffective in its substance. It is disappointing in its approach because it does not provide a constitutionally-protected charter of liberties. It is merely a timid and tepid affirmation of a political and social tradition which, for all practical purposes, carries us no farther than the prevailing tradition in unitary Great Britain. It is unnecessarily limited in its application because (1) it takes an extremely narrow view of the constitutional values that are involved in the promulgation of a bill of rights and (2) it confines such force as it has to the federal or central level of government, leaving the provinces unaffected by its provisions. It is ineffective in its substance because, taken on its own terms, its grandiloquence of expression is set in so narrow an operating framework as to rob the expression of any substantial value in concrete cases.
I could quote at length from articles in this publication by authorities taking that same stand. Indeed, I think there is only one article in this whole review that supports the bill in the form in which it was presented to them and to us, a form which is substantially the same as that which we have now before us.

maintopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman allow a question? In view of his reference to this statement that the provinces would be left unaffected by the bill of rights in its present form, will the hon. gentleman tell the house why it was that during the long period in which he was secretary of state for external affairs he did not bring before the house for approval by Canada the United Nations declaration of human rights?

maintopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question the Prime Minister asks me is why did I not bring before the House of Commons the United Nations declaration of human rights when I was a member of the cabinet. That declaration, it is known, caused some hesitation on the part of the government of that day because it included matters which were

within provincial jurisdiction. This hesitation made it impossible for us to have accepted an international bill of rights without provincial approval; but it did not prevent the government of Canada at that time accepting the United Nations declaration of human rights.
That was done; that was accepted by the Canadian representatives. It was possible for any hon. member of the house, and particularly for hon. members of the opposition, to have put on the order paper at any time during those years a private member's motion to have this matter discussed. The government did not initiate any such discussion true, but the present Prime Minister and other hon. members of the opposition of that day did not take the action open to them.

maintopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext: I asked the government about it regularly, did I not?

maintopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext: I know that the Prime Minister asked for discussion of this matter inside and outside the house, but were steps taken by the opposition to bring about a discussion? It could have been done if there existed at that time the kind of anxiety to have it done that is being expressed now.

maintopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext: Have you contacted the provinces?

maintopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext: Yes, indeed we have. My complaint is that this government is not making any effort to contact the provinces. The government has had two and one half years at least in which to get in touch with the provinces on this matter and so far as we know-and the Prime Minister can deny it if it is not correct-there has been no step taken in that direction.

maintopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext: That has nothing to do with the question I asked.

maintopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext:
The Prime Minister said that the really significant importance of this bill is the warning that is contained in it to future parliaments not to pass legislation infringing the freedoms and rights which are declared to exist in this bill. The hon. gentleman knows, of course, as we all know, that it cannot bind any future parliament. It is an ordinary piece of legislation in that sense. When I use the word "ordinary" I refer only to the technical use of the word. But while he says it cannot bind future parliaments, it will make it much more difficult for future parliaments to infringe the provisions of this bill if they feel inclined to do so.
If parliament in this country does in fact need this kind of warning we are in a bad way. Surely the fact is that no Canadian parliament would ever lightly take action of the kind we are now being warned against
Human Rights
except perhaps in time of apprehended war or emergency under the War Measures Act, which the Prime Minister and the government are not intending to change along the lines we advocated on Friday but are suggesting that the only change to be made is to have the proclamation bringing it into effect discussable in parliament.
Surely it is obvious that a warning of the kind embodied in this particular bill can be only as effective as the self-restraint, selfcontrol and self-imposed discipline of the representatives of the people make it. In our parliamentary system it is this on which we must rely. As Professor McWhinney states in the Canadian Bar Review article of March, 1959:
If the new Canadian bill of rights happens to correspond to deeply felt popular sentiments, no legislative majorities in the future are likely to interfere with it.
If it does not so correspond-then no bill now will be an adequate protection against legislative action.
In short, I doubt whether the wrong kind of parliament would be more hesitant to pass the wrong kind of legislation merely because this proposed bill of rights had become law, especially as it would be ordinary law and not embodied in our constitution. Why should a future parliament be more impressed by and respectful of this bill than it would be of historic charters of our liberties such as the Magna Carta, the petition of right of 1627, the habeas corpus act of 1640 and the bill of rights of 1689, all of which are now part of the fundamental law and heritage of Canada?
It can be argued that a reaffirmation in law of these fundamental principles will do no harm and will, in fact, do some good. Perhaps it will; yet it must be emphasized again that it fill not bind any future parliament, even though it is designed to limit and check wrong tendencies in future parliaments. It must be re-emphasized that if it is to have that deterrent effect the language of the bill must be impressive, effective and beyond doubt or uncertainty.
A distinguished lawyer in this country, Mr. Carter, writing in the Canadian Bar Review, of March, 1959 at page 261, on this idea that parliament must be warned in a bill of this kind, had this to say:
How much better it would be to trust parliament and the courts as they have been trusted in the past to modify the law relating to such private rights as circumstances and public opinion require, and not put this part of the law in a strait jacket of the model of 1959. It will be a sorry day for Canada when parliament is so distrustful of itself and its successors that it surrenders its power to change the law. Of course, the idea is absurd. If parliament in the future should decide that the law should be changed, it would simply preface its enactment by the formula

Human Rights
"Notwithstanding anything contained in the bill of rights". The prohibition in the bill against abrogation, abridgement and infringement of rights, in other words, is idle and to the layman misleading.
Well, Mr. Speaker, legal arguments aside -and I know there can be legal arguments lor and against the value of this bill-this bill, we have been told by the Prime Minister, transcends these legal considerations. It is to serve as a beacon; a red light against parliamentary carelessness or arbitrary conduct; a symbol; a great charter of liberty, or at the very least the first chapter in a charter of liberty. But if it is to be the document that we have been told by the Prime Minister it is meant to be, it should not only be broad and deep in its meaning but should be inspiring in its language; something that will stir the pulse, stimulate our national patriotism, something that could be read and be remembered by school children on July 1-

maintopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext: Does the bill of rights of the United States, or of India, do that?

maintopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext: -as one of the charters of our growing nation; something reaffirming our dedication to freedom and to great ideals; something, in short, like the declaration of the United Nations on human rights and fundamental freedoms in the international sphere, in the kind of language that should be accepted by the Canadian government.

maintopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext:
Not by parliament,
because you would not bring it before parliament.

maintopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext: Parliament could not deal with it.

maintopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext:
The Prime Minister must know that this is an international declaration, not a law, not a convention, not anything that could be ratified by parliament. The Prime Minister must know, because at any time he wished during the years he has been in opposition he could have put a resolution on the order paper affirming our acceptance of and our dedication to the ideals in this declaration. He could have done so.
This value of the bill of rights, this symbolic, inspiring value, was, among other things, exactly what the 30 national groups and associations representing a large crosssection of the people of Canada asked for when they saw the Prime Minister, I think it was in April, 1959. In their submission, which I have before me and which I wish I had time to put on the record, they did include this paragraph:
This act we feel should contain an inspiring statement of the basic rights and liberties which are part of our inheritance and to which every

person in Canada is entitled. It should, we believe, be expressed in clear, beautiful and moving language. Language that will be understood and will make a lasting impression on our children in the schools, on new immigrants who come to Canada; on all Canadians when they hear it at meetings, in court, at worship, over the radio, or on television, or read it in the press or in books.
Does this bill do that? Read its ambiguous and uninspiring language. Is it the kind of urgent, moving appeal that will be listened to by school children, or even by adults? Read it. Is it a standard that can be raised high to which men and women of this country could repair when their liberties were threatened? Read it. Does it include any of the ideals, inspiration and noble words that might be used to make a declaration which, even without any binding legal effect, would nevertheless be a landmark in our history? Does it include any of the ideas, the proposals, the words submitted to the government in the last two years, by organizations and citizens, some of which I have just quoted? Yet the Prime Minister tells us that this dry, legal document which begins, "This part may be cited as the Canadian bill of rights" without any preamble; this legal document with these dry, unexciting words, is to be the Canadian Magna Charta.
If the Prime Minister feels that way why did he not put in the preamble something worthy of the high place he gives this bill, as is done in the submission I have just mentioned? In committee we shall try to repair some of these omissions and inadequacies. Detailed criticism of the omissions and inadequacies of this bill will be given by other members on this side; and particularly, as I think will be appropriate, when the committee is set up we certainly hope to examine very, very carefully clause 2 of the bill.
The Prime Minister makes high claims for the significance of this clause. Professor Laskin, however, in his article has this to say:
Nothing except repetition is gained by setting out in the proposed bill what may be termed common law postulates of our criminal law. The postulates would not survive a deviating amendment of the code.
This clause merely declares; it does not guarantee. It creates no new offence, it imposes no penalty, no sanctions of any kind for a breach of any of its declarations. Any individual who claims his freedoms or rights have been interfered with by anyone else will be in the same position as if this bill never became law, notwithstanding the Prime Minister's eloquent assurances on television.

maintopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext: That is not a fact.

maintopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext: That is a fact.

maintopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext:
No enforcement machinery is set up, as I have said, though the Prime Minister has often talked about setting up some enforcement machinery; and in committee we may have something to say about the desirability of setting up at least some supervisory machinery.
It is true the Minister of Justice has to examine bills and regulations to ascertain whether they are inconsistent with the purposes and provisions of this legislation. In the earlier 1958 edition the Minister of Justice, under clause 4, was told "to examine legislation and regulations in order to ensure that the purpose and provisions of this part in relation thereto are fully carried out." Now, that language was pretty strong, and perhaps you could read some kind of sanction into that language; but as a result of the amendment in the present bill he does not have to examine these matters to ensure that the provisions are being carried out. All he has to do now is examine regulations and legislation to ascertain whether any of the provisions thereof are inconsistent with the purposes and provisions of this bill. That, Mr. Speaker, is a weakening of the earlier bill in regard to machinery to ensure, if it can be done, that it should be carried out.
Is the Minister of Justice accountable to parliament for the discharge of this particular duty? How do we deal with him if he fails?

maintopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext: Take out a writ of mandamus.

maintopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext:
There is another clause of the bill into which the Prime Minister has read much, which instructs-and I am paraphrasing the language-judges to interpret the law now along certain lines. That, however, hardly goes beyond the ordinary canons of judicial interpretation. Surely it does not render null and void or qualify any laws, rules or orders incompatible with the declarations of this bill. As Professor Laskin said:
The injunction to the courts to construe an enactment in conformity with the bill would not enable the courts to ignore terms that ran counter to the bill.
I wonder how the Prime Minister reconciles that statement with what he said last Thursday evening and Friday morning. The other detailed provisions and questions will be dealt with by my colleagues.
There is something more important than these detailed provisions in sections 2 and 3, and that is the general confusion that may arise over the interpretation of these provisions by the courts. Is this bill-perhaps we will get an answer to this during the course of the debate-to be interpreted as legally operative to override provincial legislation that conflicts with the rights specifically
Human Rights
enumerated in section 2? The majority of the commentators on the bill whom I have been able to study think not, but some take the other view. If the former view is the right one, then by this bill we merely confirm, underline and emphasize the fact that there are fundamental and human rights in Canada on two different levels, federal and provincial. This has caused a great deal of anxiety in legal circles.
Perhaps on this point I might read from an article by Mr. David Mundell on the Canadian bill of rights included in the bar review at page 256. In this article, he is dealing with this particular point, and he says:
To some persons the bill is to be interpreted as legally operative to override provincial legislation. To others, since the language is in terms declaratory only and not directly mandatory and since section 3 is restricted to federal legislation, the bill is to be interpreted as intended to be restricted in its effective legal operation to federal legislation. Support has been given to this view by statements that have been made.
The intended effect of the bill should be made clear, to enact it knowing that a basic question of interpretation which can be avoided will arise at the outset, is undesirable. The adoption of the principle of the declaration appears to make it logical to give it its fullest possible legal effect as overriding inconsistent provincial legislation.
This is a very important point which certainly should be cleared up. It could have been cleared up if this bill or a draft had been submitted to the supreme court for an opinion, as the Prime Minister himself once thought should be done. Arising out of these views expressed by Mr. Mundell and others, the question was asked at the bar association meeting and in the committees which were dealing with this matter, and a recommendation was made to refer this to the supreme court for a decision on this vital question of constitutionality.
Well, Mr. Speaker, this is the new bill. The few changes that have been made from the old bill are, as I have suggested, not of major importance. One or two of them, I think, do extend the bill and are perhaps helpful from that point of view, but one or two of them are retrogressive in character. We ask ourselves, therefore, on July 4, I960, is this all we have to show; is this all the government has to show for the consideration presumably given from September, 1958 to July, 1960? Is this all the government has to show for all the submissions, all the evidence and all the statements that have been made concerning this matter?
I think it is also true to say, Mr. Speaker, that the few changes that have been introduced-in fact I know it is true to say______are
not the result of public hearings, because none have been held, or of examination by a committee of parliament, because none

Human Rights
has been set up. What a commentary that is on the government's public statements about the seriousness and importance of this subject for all Canadians.
I repeat that we on this side of the house do not underestimate the seriousness or importance of the subject in any way. We do criticize both the declaration and the bill, and the effectiveness of the government's handling of the whole matter once the Prime Minister and the government decided to proceed by way of legislation.	.
May I conclude, Mr. Speaker, with one or two very general and very short observations. In recent years the asserted claims of the individual on the state have been matched by his protests against the state's interference in his activities and in his private life, an interference which his own demands have made easier and in some cases inevitable. The state cannot provide services and support for the citizen without acquiring the power and authority which is necessary and desirable for that purpose. Put it another way; more social security, desirable and even necessary though that is, may often be the means to greater state powers, and the latter persistently press against the freedom and rights of citizens who are to benefit from these powers.
Now, that pressure is often embodied in masses of legislation and regulations which are required; often so great and complicated a mass that only with difficulty can it be reconciled to the equal necessity of defining and protecting the rights of an individual against the state from which he demands these services and this protection. This is the great dilemma of a democracy in the changing circumstances of today. Its resolution in the interests of the individual is not going to be easy whatever kind of legislative action we may or may not take. It will require careful and continuous watching and safeguarding by an alert and vigilant public opinion expressed in a very alert and vigilant parliament.
It will require, above all, strict adherence to the principle that the rights of the individual are paramount and cannot be subjected to official interference and limitation unless such official action can be unmistakably justified on the grounds of overriding public interest or national security. In this essential protection of our rights and our freedoms, words, declarations and even laws are not enough. At times they are nothing at all. History shows that. It also shows that in this matter the spirit is greater than the word; that custom and convention can be more powerful even than the law. It is the British tradition and the British instinct to rely on these intangibles, traditions, customs,

opinions. That British instinct and that British tradition which we have inherited in these matters is based upon, and I think justified by, experience. If these intangibles go wrong everything goes wrong and no law will save us. It is also this instinct and this tradition which have encouraged us to rely on parliamentary action in specific cases for specific purposes to protect our rights and our freedoms, rather than to rely on any fundamental law above and beyond parliamentary control.
Well, Mr. Speaker, the record over the years is certainly not perfect. However, I think it has in the past justified this approach and adherence to these principles which are grounded in the sovereignty of a free and democratic parliament. In this bill we are departing from this British tradition. New circumstances, new difficulties and new pressures may justify some such departure, but they will not justify the limited, confused and uncertain departure embodied in this bill. Exaggerated language, extravagant claims and window dressing can only add to the confusion; they cannot supply a justification.

maintopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the very fact that the Canadian parliament has under consideration a bill to provide for the protection of basic human rights and fundamental freedoms is, in my opinion, in keeping with world feeling on this question. Some of us who watch the affairs of man as they unfold from day to day cannot help but be discouraged at abridgements of human rights and fundamental freedoms when they occur, and cannot help but be concerned and disappointed when there are setbacks. However, at an ever increasing pace I think mankind is going forward to a higher plane of human relations, and that all over the world, with few exceptions, human rights and fundamental freedoms are on the increase and are receiving greater and greater recognition.
Those of us who discuss this bill will have in mind many types of rights and fundamental freedoms. Some are mentioned in the bill; others are not referred to. These rights include the right of the individual to protection of the law without discrimination by reason of race, national origin, colour, religion or sex; freedom of religion; freedom of speech; freedom of assembly and association; and freedom of the press.
The whole question of human rights and fundamental freedoms has been a matter of long, careful and frequent discussion by the Canadian House of Commons. Participating in this discussion over the years have been many distinguished Canadian parliamentarians.

The Prime Minister introduced his bill of rights last Friday, and it is being discussed again today. He will take satisfaction in the distance he feels that it is moving toward the betterment or greater protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms. The Leader of the Opposition, in a very full and informative statement, has placed his ideas on Hansard in this regard. I have the honour today to follow in the long and consistent tradition of the C.C.F. party in supporting a bill of rights and in supporting guaranteed human rights and fundamental freedoms.
As a matter of fact, looking back through the record of Hansard, I find that the first resolution having to do with the proposition that there should be a bill of rights in Canada was moved in this house in 1945, as reported at page 900 of Hansard of that year, by Mr. Alistair Stewart, who was at that time the member of parliament for Winnipeg North. His resolution, presented some 15 years ago, is extremely interesting in that it points out some of the important questions relating to human rights and fundamental freedoms being debated at this very time. The resolution reads as follows:
That, in the opinion of this house, there should be incorporated in the constitution a bill of rights protecting minority rights, civil and religious liberties, freedom of speech and freedom of assembly; establishing equal treatment before the law of all citizens, irrespective of race, nationality or religious or political beliefs; and providing the necessary democratic powers to eliminate racial discrimination in all its forms.
This motion was presented at that time and debate was postponed because of the assurance of the present hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) that a citizenship bill would be introduced that would go at least part way in providing these important human rights and fundamental freedoms. Then in 1947 Mr. Stewart went on to discuss this question and, in a paragraph that I feel points out very adequately the choice of this parliament and for the matter the choice of mankind, he had this to say, at page 3161 of Hansard for that year:
We realize that there are two paths ahead, either one of which we as free agents may choose to follow as we will. One path leads to heights of splendour yet undreamed of; the other to the darkness of hatred and strife. One leads to a realm where the human spirit will rise, triumphant over the bigotries and persecutions of our age, where racial discrimination and intolerance of another's religious beliefs will be regarded as crimes against all mankind; where freedom of speech will be the inalienable right of every citizen; where men will no longer exploit their fellowmen for private gain; where every man will be master of his soul. That is one path we can choose.
The other path can lead only to that spiritual desolation to which our enemies would have consigned us.
Human Rights
Canada, I think chooses the first path outlined in this statement. As ideas of what might appropriately be done toward the greater protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms were revealed in this house the national leader of this party, Mr. M. J. Coldwell, the then member of parliament for Rosetown-Biggar, placed on the order paper a resolution which supported the amending of the Canadian constitution as a most appropriate means by which we could protect human rights and fundamental freedoms. His motion was debated in 1955. At that time I believe there were three motions on the order paper, one by the present Prime Minister, one by Senator Croll and one by Mr. Coldwell. By arrangement this motion standing in Mr. Coldwell's name was moved as an amendment. It reads as follows:
That, in the opinion of this house, immediate consideration should be given to the advisability of "the taking of whatever steps are necessary to amend the British North America Act so as to include therein the following heading and sections:
XII Human Bights
148. Notwithstanding anything in this act, it shall not be lawful for the parliament of Canada or the legislatures of any of the provinces to make laws;
(a)	Abridging freedom of speech and expression, or freedom of religion, or of the press or other means, of communication or the right of lawful assembly, association or organization.
(b)	Depriving any person of life or liberty by arbitrary or abusive measures, or denying to any person the equal protection of the laws.
(c)	Requiring or imposing excessive bail or cruel or unusual punishment or exiling Canadian citizens.
(d)	Subjecting any person to unreasonable interference with his or her privacy, family, home or correspondence.
(e)	Subjecting any person to arbitrary arrest or detention or denying to any person the right after arrest to be informed promptly of the charges against such person and to trial within a reasonable time or to be released.
(f)	Suspending the right to habeas corpus or depriving any person of a fair trial or the right to be represented by counsel".
The C.C.F., elected as the government of the province of Saskatchewan, lost no time in bringing forth a bill of rights and placing that measure in the laws of the province of Saskatchewan. So the C.C.F. movement has been consistent over the years in doing everything possible to protect human rights and fundamental freedoms.
Mr. Speaker, we are prepared at this time to give consideration to the bill which is before the house. The Prime Minister has said it is a step toward guaranteeing the more adequate protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms, but we believe it is not the most adequate measure which could be adopted. We believe the government has not prepared the ground for the bringing in of a constitutional amendment, which would

Human Rights
have provided a much more secure guarantee of human rights and fundamental freedoms. In other words we think this bill is hesitant, inadequate and merely a feeble attempt to do that which is required to be done and which can be done in adequate measure only by an appropriate amendment to the Canadian constitution.
Over the years there have been many occasions in this country when human rights and fundamental freedoms have been abridged. There was the famous Alberta press act which was set aside. There was the interference which took place with the religious freedom of Jehovah's Witnesses. We have had indications in recent years of discrimination in this country against people whose skin is coloured. We had instances in Canada at the time of the last war and following it in which there was great discrimination against Canadians merely because of the colour of their skin. There were great debates in this House of Commons when the Liberal government of the day was taking action to deport Japanese Canadians and to disperse Canadians of Japanese origin all across this country. In taking that action at that time they were supported by members of the Conservative party who were then in opposition. They were supported by certain members of today's cabinet; but in all those debates at all times the members of the C.C.F. group supported the rights of Japanese Canadians to equal treatment with other Canadians, and opposed the discriminatory action which was taking place.
Mr. Speaker, one of the leaders in this battle to protect the rights of Japanese Canadians was Angus Maclnnis, who for many years, from 1930 to 1953, was the member for Vancouver East and from 1953 to 1957 was the member for Vancouver-Kingsway. Many members of the house at that time felt that Mr. Maclnnis was not only wrong in his attitude but was committing political suicide. His constituents continued to support him over the years, however, and not long ago he was singled out for distinction by being given an honorary doctor of laws degree by the University of British Columbia in recognition of his strong and consistent fight in support of equal rights for Canadians no matter of what racial origin, no matter of what religion and no matter of what colour.
So, Mr. Speaker, I think it is very appropriate that Canada should at this time go forward once again with other nations of the world in providing greater security for human rights and fundamental freedoms. The question before us is, will this measure guarantee those human rights and fundamental freedoms ih an adequate manner?

One of the criticisms most often advanced about this type of measure is that it is merely an amendment to a statute law, that it can be amended by any parliament at any time and in any way, and that it does not provide for full and adequate protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms in the days ahead. There is also the argument that a measure of this kind does not protect Canadians from rights which have been interfered with by laws already on the statute books of this country.
I think the Prime Minister is of the opinion that this law will be passed at this session of parliament, and that it will supersede laws passed heretofore which at present interfere with human rights and fundamental freedoms. I trust that is the correct interpretation of this bill and that it is the interpretation which will be placed on this measure by the courts.
Mr. Speaker, I have in my hand an excerpt from a submission by the Canadian Jewish congress conference on human rights which took place in Ottawa on December 8-10, 1958. In the course of this conference they had this to say:
To say, as Bill C-60-
That was the predecessor of this bill.
-says, that all acts of parliament "shall be construed and applied" as not to abridge the rights and freedoms declared therein may mean no more than that they shall be interpreted compatibly with these rights and freedoms if such an interpretation is not inconsistent with the express terms of those acts. Nothing would be changed by Bill C-60 where by express provision an act of parliament spoke in contrary terms.
Here is an opinion which says that with the passage of this bill it will not supersede previous acts of parliament where there is a special and clear conflict in terms. That is a very severe condemnation of the value of the bill now before the house.
Mr. Speaker, may I call it one o'clock?
At one o'clock the house took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at 2 p.m.

maintopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext:
When we rose at the luncheon adjournment I had quoted from the submission of the Canadian Jewish congress in which the congress stated that in its opinion this bill would not protect human rights and fundamental freedoms when these were at odds with the provisions of acts of this parliament which had already been passed.
The second criticism of the strength of this bill is that when it becomes an act it will

be possible for parliament, by a simple step, to contravene the guarantees contained in the measure. Professor Bora Laskin of Toronto university has the following to say on this point:
Section 4 of Bill C-60-
That is the present bill's predecessor
-states that the Minister of Justice shall examine every draft bill introduced in the house and every regulation so that they shall not contradict the declarations of part I of Bill C-60. His failure to do so in, any particular case will not, I suggest, affect the validity of an act of parliament and beyond this, the legal power of parliament to ignore the terms of Bill C-60 in any future legislation is unquestionable.
An amendment to the constitution would remove the possibility of parliament, by the enactment of a simple statute, contravening the guarantees contained in such a constitutional provision. The weakness of this measure as it stands is that parliament, by a simple act, many remove the benefits that are stated to flow from this legislation when it becomes law.
There is a further criticism I wish to make on the same ground. Not only does this bill, as I see it, not endeavour to protect Canadian citizens against an infringement of their rights by way of provincial legislation, but it does seem to me that it may well exclude provincial acts from the effects of this present measure. In other words this act, if passed, might make it easier for provincial legislatures to interfere with the rights of Canadian citizens in the various provinces. My reason for saying this is the wording which appears in clause 3 of the bill:
All the acts of the parliament of Canada enacted before or after the commencement of this part, all orders, rules and regulations thereunder, and all laws in force in Canada or in any part of Canada at the commencement of this part-
Here are the qualifying words:
-that are subject to be repealed, abolished or altered by the parliament of Canada, shall, unless it is otherwise expressly stated in any act of the parliament of Canada hereafter enacted, be so construed and applied as not to abrogate, abridge or infringe-
And so on. It seems to me that this provision opens the door wide for provincial governments if they should so desire, to abridge human rights and fundamental freedoms by precisely excluding acts of that kind from the effects of this measure.
It has already been stated in this debate that there is one provision in this bill which seems a good deal weaker in its substance than the corresponding provision in the bill which was presented to us on a former occasion. I refer to clause 4 of Bill No. C-60, the first bill introduced on this subject on September 5, 1958, in which it was stated:
Human Rights
The minister of justice shall, in accordance with such regulations as may be prescribed by the governor in council, examine every proposed regulation submitted in draft form to the clerk of the privy council pursuant to the Regulations Act and every bill introduced in the House of Commons, to ensure that the purpose and provisions of this part in relation thereto are fully carried out.
That would seem to be a clear directive from parliament to the Minister of Justice to make absolutely certain that no future bills introduced in this house should contravene the provisions of the act. However, clause 4 of the present bill has changed the operative words, which now read:
... in order to ascertain whether any of the provisions thereof are inconsistent with the purposes and provisions of this part.
Well, should the minister find that certain provisions in a bill do contravene or are inconsistent with the purposes and provisions of the part of the act mentioned, that does not prevent him from recommending that such legislation should nevertheless be presented to this house, and does not ensure, as the former bill said must be ensured, that "the purposes and provisions of this part in relation thereto" are fully carried out.
In the light of this clause of the bill it would appear that after waiting for almost two years, instead of obtaining a more adequate bill stronger in its terms and in its protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms, we have a bill that is in fact weaker in its phraseology and its instructions to the Minister of Justice.
We are debating this bill in the concluding days of this session. I do not know how one could do it, but I think there should be some kind of legislation to assure that statements made by the government and its representatives and by the Prime Minister are in fact lived up to and carried out. When saying that the bill of rights would be laid over to the next session the Prime Minister, as reported at page 6293 of Hansard of July 18, 1959, had this to say:
In saying that I want to make clear that from the suggestion I have to offer to postpone the introduction of the bill of rights until the beginning of the next session-
That was the clear understanding. This bill was to be introduced at the beginning of this session, and during this session a committee was to be set up to study the provisions of the bill. Over a long period of time, perhaps over a substantial part of the session, the committee was to have the right to hear witnesses and evidence and decide whether or not the bill in an improved form could be brought into the house. The Prime Minister will not argue that the legislation was not ready, because there have been so few amendments that one might say it was almost ready in this form on September 5, 1958.

Human Rights
I have in my hand a copy of the bill that I take it was in final form, in the view of the appropriate officers of the house. This is an advance copy of the bill to which reference has already been made in the daily press, and it is stamped January 12, 1960. In other words the bill was available and printed on January 12 of this year. Where was it hidden? It was put away in somebody's closet. The Prime Minister denied this bill to the House of Commons for six months, and failed to carry out the terms of his undertaking given to this house.
In the light of the hopes of Canadians and the fight the Prime Minister has waged over many years for a bill to guarantee human rights and fundamental freedoms, this is a pale image of the legislation the Canadian people had hoped would be introduced at this time. There seems to be a great difference between the way hon. members of the government act when in government and the way they spoke and acted when in opposition.
On previous occasions I have referred to the way this government has failed to protect human rights and fundamental freedoms under the constitutional power it now holds. One of the darkest events in Canadian history was the passing in the province of Newfoundland of certain labour laws. Although an application was made to the governor in council requesting that this legislation be set aside, the Prime Minister refused to set it aside as we think he should have, and failed to be frank with parliament by telling us the decision was made. The hon. gentleman procrastinated and evaded when asked what the government would do until a year had elapsed. The legislation remains in effect. This is not the attitude of a government that is sincerely endeavouring at all times to protect human rights and fundamental freedoms.
One does not expect that this government can have jurisdiction in any way over the citizens of other countries. We are part of the United Nations organization. We have taken a strong stand on previous occasions with respect to certain questions respecting human rights and fundamental freedoms. When we saw some months ago a shocking revelation of racial prejudice and discrimination in South Africa, some of us raised this question in the house. We asked Canada through the government and the Prime Minister to take a strong stand on the issue. The government did not stand in favour of racial discrimination, but there was hesitancy. The question was evaded. Many months went by before the Prime Minister made a statement. In some ways it was a peculiar statement.

It contained a peculiar sentence which I think is a shocking reflection of the attitude of the Prime Minister toward human rights and fundamental freedoms in South Africa. I quote from the Prime Minister's statement as reported at page 3088 of Hansard of Monday, April 11, 1960:
I would also point out that if I were not sitting where I am, with the responsibilities that are mine, I would express myself somewhat differently from the way I am at the moment.
That may well be a true statement. If it is true it must mean that there is one attitude taken by the Prime Minister in opposition and a weaker attitude taken by him when in government.

maintopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext:
I accept your ruling, Mr. Speaker, as I always do. I have no further

remarks to make on that subject. In a discussion of the question of human rights and fundamental freedoms I feel it is appropriate to refer to the lack of those rights in other parts of the world, so long as there is some connection between that situation and what is happening in Canada or statements that are made in this house from time to time.
We in this party have argued for a long time that what is required by way of protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms is a constitutional amendment. 1 do not know whether the Prime Minister is opposed to a constitutional amendment; it is very difficult to find out. But if the Prime Minister is opposed to a constitutional amendment then he is acting in a very consistent manner; because at page 5650 of Hansard he said in reply to a question of mine as to whether the government had considered approaching the provinces to obtain agreement on a constitutional amendment that he had not consulted the provinces and I quote:
Mr. Speaker, one has only to review the discussions that have taken place at the several dominion-provincial conferences in recent years, and as a matter of fact throughout the years to give a completely effective answer to that question.
If that is the effective answer, it is that the Prime Minister did not canvass the provinces, that he did not try. At least one province suggested to the government that such a canvass of the views of provincial governments should be undertaken. The premier of Saskatchewan, in a lengthy letter dated January 19, 1959, wrote to the Prime Minister asking that such a course be followed, and in so doing he had this to say:
For these reasons, I urge you to reconvene the constitutional conference of federal and provincial governments which was held in 1950 and to submit to it your proposals for an amendment to the constitution which will contain a statement of human rights and fundamental freedoms in clear and explicit form.
As far as I can tell from the return that was brought down-and the Prime Minister will correct me if I am wrong-the Prime Minister himself, over his own signature, has not yet replied to that letter. I make that statement because on June 23, in reply to a motion of mine for the production of papers, this correspondence was produced and the only answer in the correspondence is one dated June 22, 1959, addressed to the premier of Saskatchewan and signed "Respectfully, Gowan T. Guest, executive assistant and private secretary" to the Prime Minister. I know the Prime Minister is a busy man. I know that from time to time, because of public business, he is outside of Ottawa, but I do not think it is an indication of good federal-provincial relations for the Prime
Human Rights
Minister himself not to have made an immediate reply, or if out of Ottawa, then in a relatively short period of time, to this important submission to him by the premier of Saskatchewan.
In our view these are the things that the government should have done; it should have explored every possible avenue to the end that an amendment to the constitution of this country, agreed to by the provinces, might be brought in.
Many important submissions have been made on this question, one of them made by Professor Bora Laskin, who argues, and I quote his words:
Enough has come from the courts to suggest that if there is any dominating authority in the area of civil liberties it is that of the parliament of Canada and not of the legislatures of the provinces.
He goes on to show that in his view parliament should act in a field that is clearly within its jurisdiction. Mr. Justice Thorson of the Exchequer Court of Canada makes a statement along the same lines:
But it seems to follow, under our federal system which divides the field of self-government in the manner which I have stated, that since the legislative assemblies of the provinces cannot abridge these freedoms, the parliament of Canada can validly do so. There is strong support for the view that these freedoms, at any rate, ought to be embedded in our constitution by an appropriate amendment of the British North America Act so that not even the parliament of Canada can detract from them. And it would seem to follow from what I have said that parliament could properly seek such an amendment without prior approval of the provinces, since the subject matter of the amendment is not within their legislative competence.
Therefore we have the views of many learned authorities who believe that the course taken by the government today is a the very best a second course, and not the more preferable one that is available to the government. This afternoon we have been talking about certain human rights and fundamental freedoms. We have been talking about freedom of speech, of assembly, of the press and of other freedoms that we usually refer to. Professor Frank Scott, in his very interesting series of articles on the Canadian constitution and human rights, after an elaborate inquiry into what can be done to better protect those rights, ends his series of articles and broadcasts with these words:
If we are going to put anything into the constitution I hope we shall put in economic and cultural rights as well as the basic freedoms. We live in the age of the positive state, not the negative state, and it is important that we keep before us the democratic goals toward which all state power should be aimed.
In other words, Mr. Speaker, in the development of human rights and fundamental freedoms it is the opinion of this authority

Human Rights
on our constitution and of other authorities around the world that the time has now come when economic freedoms should be added to the list of what we might call traditional freedoms.
