Human Rights
The day the United Nations charter was signed by 50 nations, on June 26, 1945, mankind entered into a new phase. International protection was no longer a dream and the future, for all peoples of the earth, was turning towards new destinies.
The United Nations now look after the protection and respect of our rights and of our fundamental freedoms.
Canadians now wish to achieve the realization of the principles of the United Nations charter, which specified the fundamental rights belonging to each man, in the social and legal field.
That great doctrine of human freedom was clearly set out by Pius XI in his encyclical entitled Divini Redemptoris.
Human beings must rank first among earthly realities.
And Pius XII went still further, in a letter written to the president of the social weeks of France, on July 14, 1946:
In the last analysis, everything must tend and converge toward the liberation of human beings. It is those creatures that God placed on top of the visible universe, making of them, both in economics and in politics, the measure of all things.
On April 14, 1945, that is, a month before the signature of the United Nations charter, the executive committee of the Canadian Episcopate stated:
Always, throughout history, the things that have compromised world peace have been the unfair treatment of minorities, the denial of civil and religious liberties, and other denials of man's innate right.
In 1946, 18 member states of the United Nations set up a commission called upon to prepare recommendations towards the development .of a charter of human rights. That commission was composed of a theologian, a jurist, sociologists and moralists. Its work was to be divided in three parts:
(1)	To draft a statement establishing the limits of human rights;
(2)	To prepare a pact, to be signed by the various states, giving legal effect to such rights;
(3)	To prepare means of enforcing and guaranteeing such rights.
In February 1947, the commission held its first meeting in Lake Success and, under the chairmanship of Mrs. Roosevelt, submitted a report of its recommendations. The first to promote the principles of that commission before the United Nations were Brazil, Lebanon and the Netherlands. And the representatives of those countries concluded:
The responsibility of the state is to regulate human rights in the social exercise.

speakeroldname: Mr. M. J. A. Lambert (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak on this bill at this time. It is not my intention to rehash the arguments

Human Rights
that have been so ably put forward by hon. members who preceded me. However, having heard some of the things hon. members have said I feel compelled to say something in at least partial reply.
I was most interested in what the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) had to say and as a lawyer I was pleased to see that he had reached deeply into the writings of members of the profession and drawn at least some of his inspiration from contributions to the Canadian Bar Review. However, bearing in mind that these contributions appeared in the March, 1959 issue of that publication it is instructive to read the proceedings of the annual meeting of the Canadian Bar Association held in Vancouver in September of last year. I would direct the attention of hon. members to the publication of those proceedings wherein starting at page 85 there appears the report of the civil liberties section. Frankly one would expect that among lawyers there would be some crystallization of the opinion on the question of the bill of rights.
I recall attending the annual meeting of the Canadian Bar Association held in Toronto in September of 1958 shortly after the first draft of the bill had been presented to this honourable house for consideration by the representatives of the Canadian people. Perhaps it was because the election of 1958 was so recent, but unfortunately it seemed to me that at that time a certain element of partisanship was injected into the consideration given this bill. Members of the association present at the time did not approach this matter objectively. It was finally concluded that members of the association could go back home and study the bill. We observed with what result. Having let their partisan feelings die down and become more dormant they considered the question more dispassionately and we have the articles that resulted including those, for example, that appeared in the March, 1959 issue of the Canadian Bar Review.
I was amused while doing some research for material for use in these few minutes at my disposal to find traces of book mice in copies of the proceedings of the 1958 convention. I do not know what the habit is that leads people to draw lines down the side of the pages of library books. Strangely enough the book mouse whose traces I discovered must not have been of our persuasion because every passage which aroused the interest of the book mouse were of those who disagreed with the viewpoint expressed by the author of the bill.
It must have been the hon. member for Restigouehe-Madawaska (Mr. Van Horne).

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
I do not think I would undertake to embarrass the hon. gentleman by indicating the identity of the person I think was the imitator of mice and who left his tracks behind.
Let us look at the resolution put forward by the civil liberties section of the Canadian Bar Association, which reads:
Whereas It is apparent that there is a wide divergence of opinions of the members of the section on the subject of a bill of rights.
And whereas it is imperative that the views of the association should be presented to the joint committee of the houses of parliament appointed to consider a bill of rights.
And whereas it would appear desirable that the views so presented should be those of the association as a whole and not only those of a section thereof.
Be it resolved, therefore, that this section on civil liberties recommends to the council and executive that appropriate steps be taken to ensure that the views of the association-*
An amendment is inserted-
"And to include those articles appearing in the March, 1959 issue of the Canadian Bar Review" be presented to the joint committee as the opportunity may arise.
Those were the conclusions of the Canadian Bar Association. I recognize that inevitably there will be honest differences of opinion on a question of such vital importance as that of our civil rights. This question goes to the very root of our being and so we cannot help but differ in opinion to at least some degree.
I believe that the Leader of the Opposition indicated that he was in sympathy with the end purpose of the bill but that he had some differences with respect to the means whereby that end would be achieved. It will always be thus, but no better means within the limitations of our Canadian constitution has yet been suggested.
Again referring to the proceedings of the annual meeting of the Canadian Bar Association, at page 92 of the report there is an indication of the viewpoint of the legal profession of Canada with respect to the bill of rights:
Now, in civil liberties, the views that are expressed in this association with regard to a bill of rights roughly categorize themselves into four basic views. Those who contend that we shouldn't tamper with it at all, that no legislation is necessary and we will leave it to the developing jurisprudence. Those that like the former bill. Those who say, "Well, a statute is fine but it should be amended." And those (who)-insist or contend for a basic amendment to the British North America Act.
For those who contend that we should not tamper with the present situation at all but should look with confidence to Great Britain where the civil rights we possess had their origin I suggest we should examine their situation to see whether or not there is need

lor a bill of rights. If hon. members want some very instructive reading I commend to their attention a book entitled "Laws and Orders" by Sir Carleton Allen which followed the book entitled "The New Despotism" by Lord Hewart. There hon. members will see just what can take place under an unwritten constitution. Those hon. members who were in Great Britain during the war will remember regulation No. 18 (b). Those who are lawyers with an academic bent will also recall the famous case of Liversidge v. Anderson.
Regulation 18(b) gave the secretary of state the power to detain any particular person- and I paraphrase-if satisfied that it was necessary to do so. True enough, this was under conditions of war and terrible war, and conditions may be somewhat different. But I think everyone will agree with me, as I agree with the author of this learned text, that regulation 18(b) disappeared none too soon from the statute books of Great Britain. There were other regulations made under their food control-and here it is elementary -any law or any regulation made under any statute should be published and should come to the knowledge of the people who are governed by such laws. And yet food regulations were passed in Great Britain during the war which had written into them, notwithstanding the fact that this regulation was not even published, "it shall be operative, and there will be an offence committed under these regulations by any breach thereof notwithstanding any nonpublication." I know of cases where people were actually convicted who did not even know, had no possible chance of knowing, that such a regulation existed. These are the things that we must guard against. Again, gentlemen, may I commend to you a reading of this text. It will show you what can happen.
No one here will deny that there have been excesses. After all to err is human and we are human; but because we have erred in the past-and I say this without any sense of partisanship-because there have been errors committed in the past and errors could be committed today and errors will be committed tomorrow, is that any argument for not putting on our statute books, in so far as we are empowered in the federal jurisdiction to do so, a statute which will relieve as much as we can against such a form of tyranny? We cannot say that this is perfect; otherwise, long before now this world would be perfect. This group, this nation, has not a sudden monopoly of superintelligence.
However, in commenting further, the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) this afternoon stated that this bill will not create
Human Rights
anything-and I am paraphrasing my notes of what he said-people will not realize that this is anything important; that it will not affect their daily lives. What does he want, something that sticks out like the Income Tax Act or the Criminal Code? People are not so conscious of habeas corpus or writs of mandamus, and yet they do know they exist, that they protect. If you asked the average man, what about habeas corpus, I think he would scratch his head and say, what is it? But yet it does exist. The hon. member further said that this should be something more than just a fizzling squib. I suggest to you that this is a beacon; this is something toward which we are pointing.
Human rights and civil rights are not something that you can cram down people's throats. I do not know-the hon. member did not suggest what he had in mind or how he could go about it-whether he wanted something dressed up in fancy language that sounded sonorous. This is a bill in simple language, and those elemental rights which we possess are simple rights.
There are those who complain that this bill has no sanctions; how can it function? But enforceability of a bill does not require a sanction. Surely its enforceability lies in the restoration of an aggrieved right and if subsequently there may lie an action in law. That is something further upon which I do not wish to speculate.
There are others who would object that this is poor timing. Why? Because they say we will not have time to consider it. Most of the arguments that have been put forward on behalf of the opposition against this bill have come forward from the criticisms which appeared in March of 1959, and those self-same gentlemen would be invited to come forward again. Those are not short essays that have been written by those learned gentlemen, but learned discourses. If anyone wishes to go into greater detail to find out what is meant, let him read.
Is there anything to be gained by the reading of those complete essays, by the detailed examination of those self-same authors? Yes, they may be brought forward to explain in part or to elucidate on some particular aspects; but do they have to present the whole case all over again? All it means is that somebody has to go and do a little homework.
There is one final point that I should like to make. This does not exist to such a great extent or it may not exist to such a great extent in the federal jurisdiction, but there has been a tendency in the United Kingdom and here for legislation to be drafted, considered and passed under which authority is

Human Rights
delegated by parliament to boards and commissions which fulfil quasi-judicial functions and from whose rulings there is no appeal. While there may be some argument for finality in some of these matters, it is my firm conviction that that is one feature of our administration as government, be it at any level, which must be curbed rather than extended.
I hope that this bill may serve the purpose of restoring to an individual those rights which may have been removed from him by the decision of a board, commission or official, from whom it is stated that there shall be no appeal. How else can rights be restored if transgressed?
Will my hon. friend permit a question?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: Yes.

I have been following him with interest, but can he tell us how this bill will deal with rights that may in any way have been affected by decisions of administrative tribunals? What right of appeal will be given against such decisions under this bill?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: It would be my view, that under this bill if any of those rights which are enumerated in the bill, if any of those processes which have been enumerated in the bill have been transgressed the provisions of this bill could be invoked to provide an appeal against the ruling; that is my hope. I should like to hear the views of my learned friend from Essex East (Mr. Martin) on this subject.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Where in the bill does that appear, if I may ask?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
There is no definite statement, but I would say that a careful reading of section 3, combined with section 2, in the appropriate cases-I will not say in all cases -will show that this bill may be invoked to relieve against any transgressions of the rights therein enumerated.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, let me say that we have been talking a lot about rights. I would say that we must never forget that for every right there is a concomitant duty; wherever there is a right of the individual as against his fellow citizen there is a corresponding duty; wherever there is a right of the individual against the state there is a corresponding duty; wherever there is a right of the state against the individual there is a corresponding duty. As long as we do not forget that, then we will see to the fulfilment of the preservation of the spirit of civil rights.
In termination, may I quote a citation which appears on the title page of this book, "Law

and Orders", which I think is appropriate to our consideration this evening:
Amongst many other points of happiness and freedom, which Your Majesty's subjects of this kingdom have enjoyed under your royal progenitors ... there is none which they have accounted more dear and precious than this, to be guided and governed by certain rule of law... Out of this root hath grown the indubitable right of the people of this kingdom not to be made subject to any punishment that shall extend to their lives, lands, bodies or goods, other than such as are ordained by the common laws of this land or the stautes made by their common consent in parliament.
Petition of the House of Commons, July 7, 1610.

First of all, Mr. Speaker, I should like to compliment the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) and this government for again taking the lead in following the example of the province of Saskatchewan. I am afraid that this bill in its present form would be no more effective, so far as Canadian citizens are concerned in the various provinces throughout the country, than if when this government followed the lead of the Saskatchewan government in connection with hospital insurance no other province had joined in the plan.
Today we have seen member after member on the government side of the house get up and almost slavishly express his confidence in the Prime Minister. I must confess that prior to the election of 1957 I possibly shared that confidence, perhaps not to the same extent as other hon. members, in the Prime Minister. However, I must say that since that time my faith, if not theirs, has been shattered. It has been shattered for a number of reasons. One of the first reasons that comes to my mind is the year of inaction followed by no action when the rights of Canadian citizens in Newfoundland were affected. Then in spite of all the glowing speeches we heard when the Prime Minister was a member of the opposition, we see four sessions of parliament go by under this government and then in the dying days of the fourth session, amid the rush of extended hours, we finally have this bill before us for discussion. In fact, I believe this is the first time I have had the privilege of speaking in this house after ten o'clock at night.
Then more recently we have seen a violation of human rights that has shaken the world. I will admit that the Prime Minister has told us South Africa knows his opinion. I am sure that most Canadians do not, and certainly those with whom I talked are not sure what the Prime Minister's opinion is of this violation of civil rights that we have seen recently carried out so brutally in South Africa. Furthermore we still see cases in which the very livelihood of civil servants hangs

upon the words of hon. members here, without any trial or any recourse. In fact, we see that civil servants are even being denied overtime pay for the extended hours they work while we are sitting here discussing this bill of rights. In addition, they are denied the right to bargain for that, which privilege other citizens of this country enjoy.
But, both the Prime Minister and the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) admitted past mistakes. I think the words of the Prime Minister were to the effect that whatever the mistakes of the past, here is a step by which we are going on to the future. When this bill was introduced last Friday it seemed to me that the stage was set just a little too pat. It was introduced on the anniversary of Canada's birthday; all the faithful were here in greater number than normal on a Friday and the galleries were filled. I am wondering, if that was not what prompted some person to send this post card which I received this morning. The message reads:
Exercise your jaws on this for a while.
It contains a cutout of the Globe and Mail a little advertisement which reads as follows:
To flee Chauvinism non-citizen needs job and pay.
Mr. Speaker, I agree with hon. members who have spoken so far and who say that this is the first step. I was also pleased to hear the Prime Minister state so clearly that this government is willing to meet half way with any province which desires to extend this bill of rights to their provinces. I hope the example we saw two years ago with regard to hospital insurance catches on just as rapidly with regard to a bill of rights and that the provinces fall in line once the lead is taken by the federal government.
I recall the hon. member for Brome-Missis-quoi (Mr. Grafftey) saying before lunch that he greatly feared a C.C.F. bill of rights. For the benefit of the hon. member, if he is not aware of it, may I say this. At the present time we have in our provinces four Tory governments, three Liberal governments, two Social Credit governments and only one C.C.F. government; but that one C.C.F. government is the only one which for years has had on the statute books a bill of rights.
Alberta has one.

I noticed that neither the hon. member nor any others on the government side have stated just in what respect they disagree with the bill of rights that is on the statute books of the province of Saskatchewan. Several of the government members stated that new Canadians
Human Rights
are calling for a bill of rights. Not only are new Canadians calling for a bill of rights; old Canadians are calling for a bill of rights and they have been doing so for years.
I wonder whether we might not sell them a false bill of goods by just passing this bill of rights in its present form. Maybe they will think that because the federal government has passed a bill of rights their rights are protected wherever they may live in this country. Unfortunately they may find that is not so.
I note that on Friday the Prime Minister said that it is impossible at the present time to get an amendment to the constitution or to get the consent of all the provinces. I also notice that many of the government members have, like parrots, repeated that statement today. However, I have yet to see any evidence, let alone any proof, that this is so.
I should like to know which provinces object to passing a bill of rights. Certainly the province of Saskatchewan does not object because it has one on its statute books right now. Surely all the other three parties represented in provincial governments across the country believe just as much in human rights and fundamental freedoms as do the C.C.F. I maintain that we have no evidence, whatsoever, that it is impossible today to get the provinces to agree to an amendment to the constitution which would incorporate a bill of rights that would be applicable to all Canadians regardless of where they live in this country. Why should we at this time pass what in effect will be not much more than an empty shell?
I notice that just in this session the Prime Minister and the government were able to get the ten provinces to agree to an amendment to the constitution with regard to judges' retirement. Surely if they will agree to that amendment they will also agree to something as basic as the fundamental freedoms and rights of the citizens of this country. If we fail at this time to pass an amendment to the British North America Act that will make this applicable to all Canadian citizens regardless of where they may live I would say that we will find ourselves in a position where we will have a bill of rights but it will not mean anything outside of possibly the province of Saskatchewan; however, we will have a bill of rights.

Mr. Speaker, I am extremely pleased to have the opportunity this evening to join hon. members, from all sides of the house in general support of this bill. I firmly believe that when most of the other things we have discussed and most of the other bills we

Human Rights
have passed this year will have been forgotten this bill of rights will be the memento that will make 1960 a memorable year in the history of Canada. In the concept of this bill and in its idealism we have the foremost expression of our Canadianism that we will show to the whole world.
The timing of the bill was excellent. Year after year across countless generations to come students in school will open up their history books to read that it was on July 1, I960, our Dominion day, that into the parliament of Canada was introduced one of the most important pieces of legislation ever to come before this House of Commons. And the timing is excellent in the session. Most minor things are almost through, and we now have the time, if we want to take it, in which to deal thoroughly with this vital bill. I hope every member of the house will take advantage of his opportunity to speak during the debate on this bill of rights.
It seems to me that we spend too little time in remembering how this nation was bom and of what we stand for. It was only a few years ago that this nation was settled. Why? It was settled chiefly for freedom; and no other reason can compare to that one. People from other countries came here to find freedom of worship, freedom of thought and freedom of speech. It was the people of freedom who founded this nation. No matter what we accomplish in terms of material things; no matter what riches we accumulate; no matter the power we may achieve in this world, we should always remember that our strength and our Canadianism comes from the fact that we are a free people; that we respect each other's rights and that out of freedom we have built the nation we have today.
It is a pity that this bill was not passed years ago. What a wonderful thing it would have been if the fathers of confederation could have incorporated it in the British North America Act. What a wonderful thing it would have been if it had been a part of our history all of these years, in a way in which every school child could see it and could understand it. I think part of the reason why the great immigration came to the United States of America in the first half of this century and the last half of the last century was the fact that the United States of America made clear that above all else it represented the land of the free; that there was a country to which a man could come from any part of the earth and find freedom to do as he liked within the law, and to find equality of opportunity among his fellows. That is what we missed in the first 90 years of our life; we should have spelled

out for everyone across this world to hear that we stood for freedom first, and that everything else was really secondary to that consideration.
This bill is in two parts. First of all, it is a declaration of our faith in a free Canada and of what Canada stands for in terms of rights of the individual. It is a declaration that we must show to all the world so that everyone will know how we revere the rights of man.
We talk from time to time in this house about gifts to underdeveloped countries. We discuss how we can assist new nations to develop and find the best mode of living and standards. I think more than anything else the gift that Canada has to give to the world is to be found in the fact that we have built this nation in freedom; and that in freedom is the fundamental concept of our Canadianism and our nation. We should take our declaration wherever the Canadian flag flies; wherever Canadians go they should bring with them that Canada is free; that all who live here are free; that we are bound in trust to cling to this before all else.
The first part of this bill is a declaration of basic human freedoms; it is the declaration of our people of our faith, in freedom and justice. The second part of the bill provides the sanction of our declaration. It has been said that this bill has no sanction. What more positive sanction can there be than that which is spelled out? In the future every act which comes before the courts of Canada is to be tested on this touchstone, that it must not deprive any Canadian citizen of his fundamental human rights. This will be the most important act upon the statute books of Canada. Every magistrate, every judge and every parliamentarian who from now on turns to the law of Canada must look at it through the glass of this bill of rights. Section 3 sets forth for everyone who wants to see that no Canadian may abridge the fundamental human rights of his neighbour, and that above all else in this nation we respect human freedoms and the right of the individual.
Consider the race between the ideologies of the world. The only fight we can really put up to communism and its materialistic philosophy is the fact that we are achieving the same material standards as they, or better, and are still free. We have always stood for the principle that the individual comes before the state and that is the foundation of our national heritage. Communistic nations have spread across the world the idea of economic splendour. They say if you toss the control of your life and your freedom into the pot, great economic reward will

flow from your personal sacrifice to the state. Our only answer to that is that freedom comes before all these things; we must have the right to worship the way we want; the right to say what we want, and the right to support what institutions we like and to turn down those we do not like. These are more important than any economic benefits which can be offered to any man.
Mr. Speaker, our pioneers, our first settlers came to this nation to prove just that. They left their homes in England or Scotland or Ireland; and the sunny fields of Europe to carve a new nation. They were ready to leave behind everything they had acquired to travel here where they could be free. We must never forget that.
From the point of view of practical operation the work this bill will do is chiefly as a watchdog over parliament. We will adopt this bill to govern ourselves and to provide that neither by hysteria, nor by carelessness nor by any subtle way will we cut down the rights of the Canadian citizen. We must be careful from now on about delegating powers to others. True, in our common law, in the precedents of English courts and of our own some of the basic freedoms set forth here do exist at law. Most of the safeguards set out in the bill exist somewhere in our case law. But here they provide a safeguard which no one can misunderstand, so that any individual who wants to may turn to this bill for sanctuary, and take it to the courts to seek relief.
All the freedoms are not here.
All the basic ones are.
The political ones.
The most important political freedom, and the only one which really counts, is freedom of speech, and that is here.
All the political ones are there.
All the fundamental freedoms are here, where they ought to be.
But not the economic ones.

We are not dealing with economic freedoms. This is a bill which codifies the rights of man we have been so proud of.
Without quibbling or question we will now have these rights as individuals, as Canadian citizens, and any man can go before the
Business of the House
courts with a sword to claim his rights. It will strengthen the hand of every judge, and of every lawyer who pleads the cause of the oppressed or of the man shut out from his rights as a Canadian. It strengthens the arm of freedom before the courts of this land.
Our founding fathers established here a special concept of government. It was based on the philosophy that the less government we have the better. The only purpose of government is to guarantee individual freedoms. The chief purpose we pass laws in this course is to protect each other's rights. There is no such thing as absolute freedom; everyone must sacrifice something to the common cause. We cannot all run loose around the nation, we must have law. And the laws we pass every day restrict individual freedoms to a certain extent. But the chief reason why we are here is to protect our human rights and our Canadian concept that the individual comes before the state.
Any democracy must live by rule of the majority. But majority rule is only a way of deciding issues. Majority rule does not make wrong into right. A man can be injured or persecuted by majority rule. This bill is intended to protect the individual and to guarantee he is not trampled on by the majority acting wrongly. The courts have always to some extent provided this defence to Canadian citizens in one way or another; now they have a better chance to do it than ever before.
May I call it eleven o'clock?

1.	For each year since January 1, 1956, has any revenue money of the Kitimat Indian band been spent without the consent of the council of that band?
2.	If so, upon what dates and for what purposes was each expenditure so made?
Answer by: Hon. Ellen L. Fairclough (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration):
1.	1956, No; 1957, Yes; 1958, Yes; 1959, Yes; 1960, Yes.
2.	The band revenue funds were expended during the following months for relief to band members under authority of section 66(2) of the Indian Act: 1957, May, September, October, November and December; 1958, January, February and March; 1959, April, May, June, July, August, September, October; 1960, February.
